games.explanation: Chris Sale is having a lovely bounce-back season, which the market has taken as license to price the Mets like they've already lost. That's the mistake. Sale is quietly more hittable by lefties than righties this year, and the Mets happen to run three of their better bats from that side, with Lindor in particular the kind of switch-hitter who does his real damage in exactly this look. Atlanta's own lineup is dangerous but volatile, and the simulated margin here is a single run, not the two-touchdown spread +140 implies. You're getting plus money on a game the board has already decided.

McGreevy is a pitch-to-contact righty who has quietly been a completely different pitcher depending on which box the hitter stands in, and the Cubs happen to roll out a lineup built to exploit exactly that split. Left-handed bats have tagged him for a .382 xwOBA while righties have barely scratched him, and Chicago answers with Busch, PCA, and the rest of a lefty-heavy core that punishes command guys who live over the plate. Rea is nothing special on the other side, but he does not need to be when the better team is the better team by a wide margin and the park is playing neutral in the heat. A near-coin-flip price on the club with the clearer path to five runs is the entire ballgame.

The market is pricing this like a normal division-quality matchup, and it isn't one. Boston is meaningfully the better team on both sides of the ball, and the Athletics keep running out a lineup where the on-base engine (Jacob Wilson) is carrying a .304 xwOBA that says the batting average is a mirage. Meanwhile the Red Sox have Contreras and Abreu punishing right-handed pitching all year, which is exactly the profile they're staring at tonight. At -144 you're laying a fair number to back a roughly seven-point edge, and that math works every time you can find it.

picks.explanation: The market is pricing this like Tampa runs away with it, and the projected margin says this is a one-run scrap the Rangers are very much alive in. Jax is a nightmare on righties but far more human against lefty bats, where his xwOBA-against jumps to a pedestrian .314, and Texas has the Pederson-Langford-Nimmo trio built to exploit exactly that split. Quantrill will give up his contact, but a 4-4 game in the seventh is how run lines cash, not how they lose. At -140 you're getting a coin-flip result with a free run of insurance, which is the entire reason this number exists.

Boston being three-touchdown favorites in baseball terms is how you end up on the wrong side of a one-run game you were supposed to blow open. The projected margin here is under half a run, which is nowhere near the gap the price implies, and the Athletics have enough thump in the middle of the order (Soderstrom's 50% hard-hit rate is not a typo) to keep this within the number even on a rough night. Boston's lineup is fine but not the buzzsaw the Elo gap suggests, and Rafaela plus Abreu can only carry so much water against a staff that mostly needs to avoid the crooked inning. Getting a run and a half at -125 on a game the sim has landing inside a run 61% of the time is the pitch, and the market is paying us to make it.
